A1.1.1.q: A graphic designer needs a powerful general-purpose computer at a desk for editing large images. Which device fits best?
A1.1.1.why: PCs are general-purpose computers for one person. A desktop gives the most power for the price.

A1.1.2.q: A small office wants one machine that can print, scan and photocopy to save space and money. What should it buy?
A1.1.2.why: An MFD combines printing, scanning, copying and sometimes fax in one device.

A1.1.3.q: A delivery driver needs a portable, battery-powered touchscreen device to capture customer signatures on the doorstep. Which device type is this?
A1.1.3.why: Mobile devices such as phones and tablets are portable, battery-powered and use touchscreens.

A1.1.4.q: A company needs a powerful computer that stores shared documents for all staff on its network. What is this?
A1.1.4.why: Servers provide files, apps or web pages to other computers on a network.

A1.1.5.q: A family buys a smart TV and a games console mainly for leisure. Which device category are these?
A1.1.5.why: Entertainment systems are devices mainly for leisure, e.g. consoles, smart TVs and streaming sticks.

A1.1.6.q: A shop installs networked cameras that record video of the tills all day. Which device type is this?
A1.1.6.why: Digital cameras capture photos or video digitally. CCTV is a video example.

A1.1.7.q: A courier company tracks every van's location live and plans routes around traffic. Which device type does this rely on?
A1.1.7.why: Navigation systems use GPS satellites to find location and plan routes.

A1.1.8.q: A home needs a device that connects all its gadgets to each other and to the internet. Which category does a router belong to?
A1.1.8.why: Communication devices send and receive information, e.g. phones, routers and modems.

A1.1.9.q: A smart thermostat has a tiny built-in computer that only controls heating, and it can be adjusted from a phone app over the internet. What is it?
A1.1.9.why: An embedded system is a computer built in to do one job. Connecting it to the internet makes it IoT.

A1.2.1.q: Someone uses their phone to check their bank balance, order food and stream music. Which context of use is this?
A1.2.1.why: Personal use covers everyday communication, entertainment, shopping and banking.

A1.2.2.q: A teacher sets quizzes on tablets and students submit homework through Google Classroom. Which context of use is this?
A1.2.2.why: Education use supports teaching, learning and assessment.

A1.2.3.q: Friends in different countries keep in touch through group video chats and shared photos. Which context of use is this?
A1.2.3.why: Social use is communicating and interacting with others online.

A1.2.4.q: A supermarket uses barcode scanners at the tills that update stock levels automatically. Which context of use is this?
A1.2.4.why: Retail use supports buying, selling and managing stock.

A1.2.5.q: A car factory uses robot arms and sensors to weld car bodies with almost no human input. Which context of use is this?
A1.2.5.why: Manufacturing uses computer-controlled machines, robots and sensors to automate production.

A1.2.6.q: A hospital uses wearable devices to monitor patients' heart rates and alert nurses to problems. Which context of use is this?
A1.2.6.why: Healthcare uses devices for diagnosis, treatment, monitoring and admin.

A1.2.7.q: A musician records, edits and mixes an album on a laptop with a drawing tablet for artwork. Which context of use is this?
A1.2.7.why: Creative use covers design, music, video, animation and photography.

A1.2.8.q: An online shop's warehouse uses robots to pick items and a chatbot to answer customer questions. What does this show?
A1.2.8.why: Automation and robotics are machines and AI doing tasks with little human input.

A1.3.1.q: An IT technician draws how the office PCs, switch, router, server and internet connect together. What kind of diagram is this?
A1.3.1.why: System diagrams show a system's components and how they connect.

A1.3.2.q: A developer plans the steps of a login process with decision diamonds such as 'Password correct?'. What is this?
A1.3.2.why: Flowcharts use standard symbols to show the steps and decisions in a process.

A2.1.1.q: A library uses a barcode scanner to read the codes on books as they are borrowed. What type of device is the scanner?
A2.1.1.why: Input devices get data into a computer.

A2.1.2.q: A teacher uses a projector to show a presentation to the class. What type of device is the projector?
A2.1.2.why: Output devices present results from a computer to people.

A2.1.3.q: A photographer copies a week of photos onto an external SSD to keep them safe. What type of device is the SSD?
A2.1.3.why: Storage devices keep data so it can be used again later.

A2.2.1.q: A user with limited hand movement struggles with small keys, so is given one with large, widely spaced keys. What assistive technology is this?
A2.2.1.why: Adaptive keyboards are adapted for users with physical, visual or learning difficulties.

A2.2.2.q: A blind employee needs software that reads emails and web pages aloud. What should they be given?
A2.2.2.why: Screen readers read screen content aloud for blind or partially sighted users.

A2.2.3.q: A blind programmer wants to read code by touch, character by character. Which device suits this?
A2.2.3.why: A braille display raises pins to form braille so text can be read by touch.

A2.2.4.q: A user with low vision can see the screen but needs text and images much bigger. Which assistive technology is best?
A2.2.4.why: Screen magnifiers enlarge part or all of the screen for low-vision users.

A2.2.5.q: A user with paralysis below the neck presses keys with a stick worn on their head. What is this?
A2.2.5.why: A head pointer is worn on the head so users can press keys without their hands.

A2.2.6.q: A user with very limited movement controls a computer by pressing one large button with their cheek. What is this?
A2.2.6.why: A single switch lets users with very limited movement control a computer.

A2.2.7.q: A medical secretary pauses and rewinds dictation audio with a pedal so both hands stay on the keyboard. What is this?
A2.2.7.why: A foot switch triggers an action by foot, keeping hands free.

A2.2.8.q: A user who can only move their mouth controls a wheelchair and a computer by sucking and blowing into a tube. What is this?
A2.2.8.why: Sip-and-puff switches are controlled by sucking or blowing into a tube.

A2.2.9.q: A user with motor neurone disease moves the cursor just by looking at different parts of the screen. What technology is this?
A2.2.9.why: Eye tracking uses a camera to follow where the user looks and moves the cursor there.

A2.2.10.q: A student with dyslexia has Word read their essay out loud to help them spot mistakes. Which assistive technology is this?
A2.2.10.why: Text-to-speech reads written text aloud as speech.

A2.3.1.q: A video production company needs to store 40 TB of 4K footage. Which storage characteristic matters most here?
A2.3.1.why: Capacity is how much data a medium can hold, measured in GB or TB.

A2.3.2.q: A school must back up huge amounts of data on a tight budget, so it compares the price per gigabyte of HDDs and SSDs. Which characteristic is this?
A2.3.2.why: Cost compares the price of storage, especially per gigabyte. HDDs are cheaper per GB.

A2.3.3.q: A gamer replaces a hard disk with an SSD so games load much faster. Which characteristic is improved?
A2.3.3.why: Speed is how fast data is read from and written to storage. SSDs are much faster than HDDs.

A2.3.4.q: A new external drive uses only USB-C, but the office PCs have only USB-A ports. Which characteristic is the problem?
A2.3.4.why: Compatibility is whether storage works with the device's connections, OS and hardware.

A2.4.1.q: A small hairdresser writes appointments in a paper diary and counts stock by hand. What kind of data processing is this?
A2.4.1.why: Manual processing is data handled by people rather than computers: slower and more error-prone.

A2.4.2.q: Every time an item is sold, the shop's EPOS till updates the stock level with no staff input. What kind of data processing is this?
A2.4.2.why: Automatic processing is done by computers with little or no human input.

A3.1.1.q: A bank processes all of the day's payments together overnight, with no one interacting with the system. Which type of OS suits this?
A3.1.1.why: Batch OSs process groups of jobs automatically without user interaction.

A3.1.2.q: A search engine spreads each search across thousands of servers that appear to users as one system. Which type of OS is this?
A3.1.2.why: A distributed OS makes many separate computers work together as one system.

A3.1.3.q: A student browses the web while music plays and a file downloads, all at the same time. Which OS feature makes this possible?
A3.1.3.why: A multitasking OS runs several programs at once by switching the CPU between them quickly.

A3.1.4.q: A school server manages shared drives, printers and every student's login across the network. Which type of OS runs on it?
A3.1.4.why: A network OS manages shared files, printers and user accounts for a network.

A3.1.5.q: A car's anti-lock brakes must react to wheel sensors within milliseconds every time. Which type of OS is needed?
A3.1.5.why: An RTOS must respond within a guaranteed, very short time, which is vital for safety systems.

A3.1.6.q: A tablet needs an OS built for touch, battery saving and apps from an app store. Which type is this?
A3.1.6.why: Mobile OSs such as iOS and Android are designed for phones, tablets and wearables.

A3.1.7.q: A cash machine runs a stripped-down OS that only lets customers do banking tasks. Which type of OS is this?
A3.1.7.why: A single-use OS is stripped down to do one job only, which also makes it more secure.

A3.1.8.q: Fifty developers log into the same Linux server remotely at once, each with their own account and files. Which type of OS is this?
A3.1.8.why: A multi-user OS lets several users use the same system at once, each with their own account.

A3.2.1.q: Which OS role handles connecting to Wi-Fi and sending and receiving data packets using protocols?
A3.2.1.why: The OS handles network protocols, connections, data transfer and bandwidth.

A3.2.2.q: Windows blocks a suspicious program and its built-in firewall stops an incoming connection. Which OS role is this?
A3.2.2.why: The OS protects the system through access control, malware protection, encryption and a firewall.

A3.2.3.q: RAM is full, so the OS moves some data to the hard drive to keep programs running, though everything slows down. Which OS role is this?
A3.2.3.why: The OS allocates RAM, keeps programs apart, and uses virtual memory when RAM runs out.

A3.2.4.q: The OS gives each running program a short slice of CPU time in turn, so they all seem to run together. Which role is this?
A3.2.4.why: The OS shares CPU time between programs by scheduling and switching between them.

A3.2.5.q: A new printer won't work until the right software is installed so Windows can communicate with it. What is that software?
A3.2.5.why: A device driver lets the OS talk to a hardware device.

A3.2.6.q: Each family member logs into the shared PC with their own password and gets their own desktop and files. Which OS role is this?
A3.2.6.why: The OS checks who users are, stores their settings and lets admins manage accounts.

A3.3.1.q: A technician runs a program that scans for malware and another that backs up the hard drive. What type of software are these?
A3.3.1.why: Utility software maintains and looks after the computer system.

A3.3.2.q: An accountant uses Excel to build a budget spreadsheet. What type of software is Excel?
A3.3.2.why: Application software is what people use to do tasks and create things.

A3.4.1.q: A charity picks LibreOffice over Microsoft 365 mainly because there are no licence fees. Which factor drove the choice?
A3.4.1.why: Cost covers buying, licensing and running the software.

A3.4.2.q: A company refuses to keep using an old OS because it no longer receives security updates. Which factor is this?
A3.4.2.why: Security includes how well software protects data and how often it is patched.

A3.4.3.q: An architect's firm can't move to macOS because its CAD software runs only on Windows. Which factor is this?
A3.4.3.why: Compatibility is whether software works with the hardware and other software already in use.

A3.4.4.q: A school chooses a learning platform because it has built-in quizzes and plagiarism checking, which it needs. Which factor is this?
A3.4.4.why: Features means whether the software has the functions the organisation needs.

A3.4.5.q: A care home picks very simple rota software because its staff have low IT skills. Which factor is this?
A3.4.5.why: Software must fit the organisation's tasks and its users' skills.

A3.4.6.q: New design software runs very slowly on the office's old PCs. Which factor was overlooked?
A3.4.6.why: Performance is how well the software runs on the available hardware.

A3.5.1.q: A network admin types commands such as 'ipconfig' to configure servers quickly, using little memory. Which interface is this?
A3.5.1.why: A CLI is a text interface where the user types commands. It is powerful but needs commands to be learned.

A3.5.2.q: A cash machine shows a few options on screen, and users choose one at a time such as 'Withdraw cash'. Which interface is this?
A3.5.2.why: Menu-driven interfaces let users choose from a list of options. They are simple, with limited choices.

A3.5.3.q: An office worker uses windows, icons, menus and a mouse pointer to manage files. Which interface is this?
A3.5.3.why: A GUI is a visual WIMP interface: windows, icons, menus and a pointer.

A3.5.4.q: A supermarket self-checkout lets customers tap and swipe on the screen instead of using a mouse. Which interface is this?
A3.5.4.why: A touchscreen GUI is controlled by touch gestures.

A3.6.1.q: A company wants an OS it can view, modify and use with no licence fee, accepting there's no official helpline. Which should it choose?
A3.6.1.why: Open-source code is free to view and change; proprietary code is closed and usually paid.

A3.6.2.q: A business pays for Microsoft 365 rather than free LibreOffice mainly to get official support and guaranteed updates. What type of software has it chosen?
A3.6.2.why: Proprietary software is closed source and paid for, but comes with official support.

A3.7.1.q: A web designer needs icons that stay sharp at any size, from a phone screen to a billboard. Which image format suits this?
A3.7.1.why: SVG is a vector format, so it scales without losing quality.

A3.7.2.q: A podcast is shared online, where small file size matters more than perfect quality. Which audio format suits this?
A3.7.2.why: MP3 uses lossy compression for small files. WAV is uncompressed and large.

A3.7.3.q: An iPhone records a video file holding both the video and the audio in one container. Which format is this likely to be?
A3.7.3.why: MOV and MP4 are containers holding video and audio streams compressed by codecs.

A3.7.4.q: A developer releases an app for Android phones. Which file format will it be installed from?
A3.7.4.why: Installer formats are OS-specific: APK for Android, EXE/MSI for Windows, DMG for macOS.

A4.1.1.q: Field engineers need a system they can use on the move in poor light with gloves on. Which factor should drive the choice of IT system?
A4.1.1.why: User needs cover users' tasks, skills, mobility and accessibility.

A4.1.2.q: A video editing team needs PCs with at least 32 GB of RAM, a fast GPU and Thunderbolt ports. Which factor is this?
A4.1.2.why: Specifications are technical requirements such as performance, storage and ports.

A4.1.3.q: A hospital's new system must read patient records saved in the old system's format. Which factor is this?
A4.1.3.why: Compatibility is whether the system works with existing hardware, software, data and networks.

A4.1.4.q: Tablets for a sales team must support 4G and Wi-Fi so staff can connect anywhere. Which factor is this?
A4.1.4.why: Connectivity is the network and device connections the system supports.

A4.1.5.q: A firm adds up purchase price, installation, licences, support and eventual replacement before choosing a system. Which factor is this?
A4.1.5.why: Cost is the total cost of buying, setting up, running and replacing the system.

A4.1.6.q: A new system lets one person process orders that used to take three people, using less paper and time. Which factor is this?
A4.1.6.why: Efficiency is how well a system uses time, money and resources.

A4.1.7.q: An office plans when to move its data to the new system, how to test it and how to keep downtime low. Which factor is this?
A4.1.7.why: Implementation covers timescales, testing, data migration and downtime.

A4.1.8.q: A manager chooses a system because staff will be able to complete twice as many claims per day. Which factor is this?
A4.1.8.why: Productivity is how a system affects how much work staff can get done.

A4.1.9.q: A law firm only shortlists systems with encryption, MFA and audit logs that fit its existing security set-up. Which factor is this?
A4.1.9.why: Security means the system's security features and how it fits existing measures.

A4.2.1.q: A supermarket's system lowers the count of beans at each sale and automatically orders more when stock is low. What use of IT is this?
A4.2.1.why: Stock control tracks stock in real time and reorders automatically.

A4.2.2.q: Sensors in a food factory record the fridge temperature every minute with a timestamp. What use of IT is this?
A4.2.2.why: Data logging is sensors automatically recording time-stamped readings over time.

A4.2.3.q: A shop studies a year of sales data to find which products sell best in summer and decide what to promote. What use of IT is this?
A4.2.3.why: Data analysis finds patterns and trends in data to guide decisions.

A4.2.4.q: Staff write letters, keep spreadsheets, email clients and book meetings in Teams. What use of IT is this?
A4.2.4.why: General office tasks are everyday admin: documents, spreadsheets, email and scheduling.

A4.2.5.q: An architecture firm uses AutoCAD to draw building plans and Blender to make 3D walkthroughs. What use of IT is this?
A4.2.5.why: Creative tasks cover design, media production and animation.

A4.2.6.q: A gym shows online adverts only to people aged 18 to 30 living within 5 miles, then measures how many click. What use of IT is this?
A4.2.6.why: IT is used to create, target and measure adverts.

A4.2.7.q: An engineer designs a part in CAD and sends it straight to a CNC machine to be cut. What use of IT is this?
A4.2.7.why: IT designs, controls and checks manufacturing, from CAD to quality control.

A4.2.8.q: A data centre uses networked CCTV and fingerprint locks on its server room. What use of IT is this?
A4.2.8.why: IT is used for physical and cyber security, e.g. CCTV and access control.

A4.2.9.q: A company's payroll runs itself every month and a chatbot answers common customer questions. What use of IT is this?
A4.2.9.why: Automation is IT doing tasks with little or no human input.

A4.3.1.q: Customers abandon a new booking system because it is slow, often offline and hard to use on a phone. Which impact is this?
A4.3.1.why: User experience covers ease of use, performance, availability and accessibility.

A4.3.2.q: A new till system is fast for staff, but customers can no longer pay by cash, which many prefer. Which impact is this?
A4.3.2.why: A system must meet the needs of both staff and customers.

A4.3.3.q: A new system's subscription fees, upgrades and support costs keep rising each year. Which impact on the organisation is this?
A4.3.3.why: Cost is the system's cost to the organisation now and over time.

A4.3.4.q: Moving patient records to a new system takes a week longer than planned, and the clinic must close for a day. Which impact is this?
A4.3.4.why: Implementation affects the organisation through timescales, testing, data migration and downtime.

A4.3.5.q: A school keeps its old timetable system running alongside the new learning platform and links the two. Which impact is this?
options: Replacement or integration with current systems
A4.3.5.why: An organisation decides whether a new system replaces the old one or works alongside it.

A4.3.6.q: Output drops for the first month while staff get used to a new system, then rises above the old level. Which impact is this?
A4.3.6.why: Productivity often dips during a change, then improves.

A4.3.7.q: After a new system arrives, sales staff work from home two days a week and log calls digitally instead of on paper. Which impact is this?
A4.3.7.why: Working practices are the ways a system changes how staff work.

A4.3.8.q: Staff get a course when a new system launches and refresher sessions whenever it is updated. Which impact is this?
A4.3.8.why: Staff need training at launch and as the system changes.

A4.3.9.q: A company sets up a helpdesk and live chat so staff can get help with the new system. Which impact is this?
A4.3.9.why: User support is ongoing help for staff using the system.

A4.3.10.q: A new cloud system means customer data now leaves the building, so the firm adds MFA and encryption. Which impact is this?
A4.3.10.why: A new system brings new security risks that must be managed.

A5.1.q: A phone with a dedicated AI chip edits photos instantly on the device instead of sending them to a server. How does this emerging technology affect performance?
options: It makes processing faster on the device
It makes the phone unable to use apps
It removes the need for storage
A5.1.why: AI hardware, 5G and edge computing make systems faster and more capable.

A5.2.q: A fake video of a celebrity, made with AI, spreads on social media. Which implication of AI for personal use does this show?
options: Deepfakes make it harder to trust what you see
A5.2.why: AI changes personal use, including risks such as deepfakes and misinformation.

A5.3.q: A bank uses AI to flag unusual card payments, and fewer staff are needed to review transactions. Which implication does this show for organisations?
options: AI changes how they operate and how many people they employ
A5.3.why: AI changes how organisations work, e.g. fraud detection and automated screening, and affects jobs.
